top_evidence.document_title: Endoscopic submucosal dissection versus endoscopic mucosal resection for colorectal laterally spreading tumors (> 20 mm): a systematic review and meta-analysis
top_evidence.text: The reporting of this systematic review follows the recommendations of the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (Supplementary Material 1) [10]. Quality assessment: Search strategy: The risk of bias was assessed independently by two reviewers (Q.Z. and T.K.) using the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool (RoB 2) for randomized trials and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) for nonrandomized controlled studies. Disagreements were resolved by discussion or by consulting a third reviewer (T.Z.). An electronic literature search was conducted by an experienced librarian with supervision from the study's principal investigator. Multiple databases were searched from inception to 1 May 2025, to identify eligible studies. The databases searched included PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane. The search strategies employed in PubMed and Cochrane Library databases were as follows: (((colorectal tumors) OR (laterally spreading tumor)) AND (endoscopic submucosal dissection) OR (ESD)) AND ((piecemeal endoscopic mucosal resection) OR (pEMR) OR (piecemeal EMR) OR (pmEMR) OR (EMR-precutting) OR (EMR-P) OR (endoscopic piecemeal mucosal resection) OR(EPMR)). The search strategy applied in the Embase database was: (colorectal AND ('tumors'/exp OR tumors) OR laterally) AND spreading AND ('tumor'/exp OR tumor) AND (endoscopic AND submucosal AND ('dissection'/exp OR dissection) OR esd) AND (((piecemeal AND endoscopic AND mucosal AND ('resection'/exp OR resection) OR pemr OR piecemeal) AND emr OR pmemr OR 'emr precutting' OR 'emr p' OR endoscopic) AND piecemeal AND mucosal AND ('resection'/exp OR resection) OR epmr).

top_evidence.document_title: Endoscopic submucosal dissection versus endoscopic mucosal resection for colorectal laterally spreading tumors (> 20 mm): a systematic review and meta-analysis
top_evidence.text: Background Colorectal laterally spreading tumors (LSTs) larger than 20 mm are significant precursors to colorectal cancer. Endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD) and endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR) are widely used treatments, but their comparative efficacy and safety remain controversial. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to compare ESD and EMR in terms of local recurrence, perforation, and delayed bleeding for colorectal LSTs > 20 mm. Methods Following PRISMA guidelines, a comprehensive literature search was conducted in PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane databases from inception to 1 May 2025. Studies comparing ESD and EMR for LSTs > 20 mm were included. Data were extracted and quality assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale and Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool. Random-effects models were used to calculate pooled odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Results Eight studies comprising 3024 patients were included. ESD was associated with significantly lower local recurrence compared to EMR (0.62% versus 12.02%; OR 0.07, 95% CI 0.03-0.13, p < 0.01). However, ESD had a higher risk of perforation (5.38% versus 1.53%; OR 3.16, 95% CI 1.89-5.29, p < 0.01). No significant difference was found in delayed bleeding rates (3.65% versus 3.75%; OR 1.01, 95% CI 0.65-1.55, p = 0.98). Heterogeneity was negligible across all outcomes ( I 2 < 5%). Conclusions ESD significantly reduces recurrence risk for colorectal LSTs > 20 mm compared with EMR but carries a higher perforation risk. Bleeding rates are comparable between the two techniques. ESD is recommended in expert centers where technical proficiency can mitigate perforation risk, while EMR-treated patients require closer surveillance due to higher recurrence. Future studies should focus on optimizing techniques and clarifying strategies for different LST subtypes and locations. Keywords Neoplasms · Endoscopic mucosal resection · Endoscopic submucosal dissection · Recurrence · Complications

top_evidence.text: Most studies included in this meta-analysis were single-center or retrospective in nature. To minimize the risk of bias, we used the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale to assess the quality of nonrandomized studies. Furthermore, owing to missing original data, we were unable to compare the potential impact of different LST subtypes or lesion locations (e.g., proximal colon versus distal colon/rectum) on the efficacy and safety of the two techniques. Since different subtypes and locations may vary in biological behavior, technical difficulty, and prognosis (e.g., more advanced histology such as high-grade intraepithelial neoplasia or intramucosal carcinoma may increase the difficulty of en bloc resection), the absence of this information may affect the interpretation of the results. Future prospective, multicenter studies, especially those collecting detailed lesion characteristics, are needed to more comprehensively evaluate the value of ESD and EMR in different clinical scenarios.
